title: Dear Cook
description:
Dear Cook’s Illustrated,
I have long enjoyed your Magazine and, more recently, you online site too. Thank you!
One of my favorite simple recipes is the Pan-Seared Filet Mignon from May 1, 2001, in particular, the basic technique: 3 minutes in a hot pan on one side, 3 minutes on the other side, and 6 minutes in the hot oven (for medium rare). Apart from the taste, etc. (very good!), I’ve liked the simplicity of the instructions and, to a certain extent, the symmetry of the cooking times (at least for medium rare).
What I’ve tried to work on for myself, but would love to get your expert take on, is how to duplicate this basic technique for a variety of other meats. I could imagine a simple, but very handy reference table listing the foods, times on one side, times on the other side, times in the oven (ideally the same temperature for all the alternatives, but maybe not). Symmetry would be nice for remembering the times, but it’s probably not possible for all the different choices (or for different preferences for doneness).
The meats that first come to mind in this pan-seared category of simple basics are (besides filet): other steaks (like t-bone or porterhouse), pork chops (with and without the bone), pork tenderloin medallions or “filets,” lamb chops, rack of lamb (like the nice ones so readily available these days), chicken breasts (with skin, maybe boneless and skinless) and maybe thighs, butterflied Cornish hens. Slightly more elaborate instructions in the same vein might include whole beef or pork tenderloin (four “sides” rather than two).
And, of course, there are any number of pan sauces that could be recommended to go with each of the main items -- ideally, ones that could be done during the time that the meat is in the oven or resting afterwards.
Also, I imagine this kind of handy reference table could be re-cast for grilling outdoors -- charcoal and gas.
Your expertise and suggestions would be greatly welcomed here and, perhaps, by your devoted readers (and cooks and eaters).
Thank you!
Blake Gall
